Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Epidemiology
The scaphoid is the most common carpal bone that sustains more than an avulsion fracture.
Young men aged 15 to 19 years appears to have the highest propensity for injury, with an
annual incidence of 88 in 100,000 in a UK population.1,2
After age 60 years, women have a higher incidence of injury than men.3
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Anatomy
The scaphoid is the only carpal bone that bridges the proximal and distal rows.
It articulates with the radius, capitate, lunate, trapezium, and trapezoid and is almost
completely covered in articular cartilage.
The main blood supply to the scaphoid is from the dorsal radial artery. The scaphoid is largely
supplied in a retrograde fashion; therefore, the proximal pole is at highest risk of
osteonecrosis after fracture.
Therefore, proposed features of the scaphoid that may render it slow or difficult to heal
include:
Highly mobile nature in several planes (only relevant for displaced fractures)
Limited blood supply
Intrasynovial location
Cartilage coverage (lack of periosteum)
Osseous and Ligamentous Anatomy

Osseous and Ligamentous Anatomy
The scaphoid is the largest bone in the proximal row and is the only osseous link
between the proximal and distal rows. It has an oblique orientation in the carpus with a
mean intra-scaphoid angle of 40° ± 3° in the coronal plane and 32° ± 5° in the sagittal
plane.2

Approximately 75% to 80% of the scaphoid is covered by articular cartilage, limiting
overall ligamentous attachment and vascular supply. Proximally, the scaphoid articulates
with the concavity of the articular surface of the distal radius. Distally, the dorsoradial
ridge articulates ulnodorsally with the trapezoid and radiovolarly with the trapezium. The
ulnar side is almost entirely articular. A proximal articulation with the lunate and a distal
articulation with the capitate are present. A concave surface of the scaphoid articulates
with a convex radial proximal capitate.4 The remaining non-articular area serves as the
entry portal for the vascular supply (Figure 1).
Figure 1 Radial (A), dorsal (B), ulnar (C), and volar (D) photographs of the scaphoid bone.
The bottom of the images is proximal, and the top of the images is distal. Colors
represent articulations with other bones: distal radius (green), trapezium (yellow),
trapezoid (orange), capitate (blue), and lunate (red) represents proximal and the top
represents distal. (Reproduced with permission from Buijze GA, Lozano-Calderon SA,
Strackee SD, Blankevoort L, Jupiter JB: Osseous and ligamentous scaphoid anatomy: Part
I. A systematic literature review highlighting controversies. J Hand Surg Am
2011;36[12]:1926-1935.)
The complex intrinsic and extrinsic ligamentous networks have an intimate relationship
with the scaphoid.4 The scapholunate interosseous ligament (SLIL) is important to
normal carpal kinematics. It consists of three interconnecting bundles4: the dorsal region
resists palmar-dorsal translation and gapping, whereas the volar portion resists
rotation.2 Concurrent scapholunate ligamentous injuries have been described in
patients with an acute scaphoid fracture.5

The radioscapholunate ligament, also known as the ligament of Testut, lacks organized
collagen bundles but consists of an abundant network of vascular and neural structures.
Consequently, some surgeons do not consider the radioscapholunate ligament a true
ligament or mechanical structure. Most fibers pass to the proximal pole of the scaphoid,
suggesting a role in reinforcement and vascularity to the SLIL and the proximal pole of
the scaphoid.
Using micro CT, Heinzelmann et al6 found that the scaphoid bone is most dense at the
proximal pole, at which the trabecular bone is thickest and more tightly packed. The
trabeculae are thinnest and more sparsely distributed at the scaphoid waist, the location
at which most fractures occur.7
Vascular Anatomy

Vascular Anatomy
Two networks of perfusion are present in most scaphoids, one network entering volarly
to supply the distal pole and a second network entering dorsally to supply the proximal
portion.8 The radioscapholunate also may play a role in providing accessory vascular
support to the proximal pole from the volar side. Based on injection studies, the
branches of the radial artery that enter the dorsal ridge supply 70% to 80% of the entire
intraosseous scaphoid volume in a retrograde fashion.9 The dependence of the scaphoid
on a single dominant artery is thought to make the proximal pole susceptible to
osteonecrosis after fracture at the waist or proximal pole7 (Figure 2).

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Scaphoid fractures most commonly occur at the scaphoid waist.
In general, they result from a fall onto an outstretched hand. The wrist position at the time of
impact has been proposed to influence the type and location of fracture.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Most scaphoid fractures occur at the scaphoid waist. The proposed mechanism of injury
is a fall onto an outstretched arm or forceful wrist hyperextension to more than 95°.


Injury Classification
Based on a systematic review of studies that included scaphoid classification systems,
the Herbert classification was the most cited classification system, followed by the Mayo
classification system10,11 (Resource 1).
In the Herbert classification, type A fractures are considered stable and include
incomplete waist fractures and fractures of the distal scaphoid tubercle. Type B fractures
are unstable acute fractures, with type B1 being a distal oblique fracture, type B2 being a
complete fracture at the waist, type B3 being a complete proximal pole fracture, and
type B4 being a transscaphoid perilunate fracture-dislocation (PLFD). Type C fractures
are delayed unions, and type D fractures are established nonunions, including type D1,
which is a fibrous union, and type D2, which is pseudarthrosis (Figure 3).

include fractures of the tubercle and incomplete unicortical crack fractures. this fracture

The Mayo classification system divides fractures into proximal pole, waist, or distal pole
fractures. The distal pole fractures are subclassified as tubercle, intra-articular, or distal
third fractures (Figure 4).
Figure 4 Illustration shows the Cooney (Mayo) classification of scaphoid fractures, which

A large study found that distal waist fractures could not reliably be distinguished from
mid-waist fractures. Simpler classification systems seem most useful and reliably
applied, classifying scaphoid fractures as proximal pole fractures, waist fractures at any
level, and distal tubercle fractures12 (Figure 5).

In addition, scaphoid fracture classification systems do not describe how to distinguish
proximal pole fractures from proximal scaphoid waist fractures. Two of the described
definitions to determine a proximal pole fracture are a fracture line in the proximal third
of scaphoid on a PA radiograph and a fracture involving a third of the articular surface of
the scaphoid with the radius and exiting proximal to the capitolunate articulation. A
study of 57 evaluators analyzing 29 scaphoid fractures (including 5 proximal pole
fractures and 24 waist fractures) randomized whether to view CT scans.13 Substantial
agreement was present with regard to the diagnosis of proximal pole fractures, and CT
scans did not improve reliability. Another study evaluated 51 acute scaphoid fractures
based on three-dimensional modeling and found that scaphoid waist fractures that may
appear proximal on radiographs can be grouped together in the middle third of the
bone.14

Based on these studies, most scaphoid fractures can be categorized on PA radiographs
as proximal pole fractures (small fractures exiting in the scapholunate articulation), a
wide range of waist fractures (exiting in the scaphocapitate articulation), or distal
tubercle fractures (exiting in the scaphotrapeziotrapezoid [STT] articulation). This simple
anatomic classification and the Herbert classification both are fairly reliable14 (Figure 5).
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History
Most commonly a patient will present with radial-sided wrist pain after a fall onto an
outstretched hand, an axial load to the wrist, or a twisting injury.15
Physical Examination
The most common physical examination findings suggestive of a scaphoid fracture are:
Tenderness of the scaphoid in the anatomic snuffbox
Tenderness to palpation dorsally over the proximal pole
Tenderness at the scaphoid tuberosity
Pain with axial compression of the first metacarpal
Correlation of physical examination findings with radiographs is important to determine the
next steps in diagnosis or management.

Physical Examination
The most common physical examination findings of a potential scaphoid fracture are
pain in the anatomic snuffbox, pain dorsally over the proximal pole, pain on palpation of
the scaphoid tubercle, pain with axial compression of the thumb, painful thumb range of
motion, and swelling in the area of the scaphoid.16 Physical examination findings should
be correlated with radiographs. In patients with a visible fracture, displacement and
instability should be determined. A notable probability of fracture based on patient
history and physical examination with no fracture visible on radiographs is referred to as

a suspected scaphoid fracture. Distinguishing true fractures from suspected fractures is
difficult.
Imaging Studies
Four standard radiographic views (PA, lateral, oblique, and scaphoid) are used in the initial
imaging for suspected scaphoid fractures.
If these four radiographic views are normal but a scaphoid fracture is still suspected based on
mechanism of injury and scaphoid tenderness, traditional management is short arm cast or
splint immobilization with repeat imaging studies and physical examination in approximately 1
week.
Alternatively, MRI or CT within the first week of injury may be considered to expedite and
refine diagnosis.
For visible fractures, CT may help diagnose displacement (gapping, translation, or angulation).
Radiography

Radiography
Initial imaging studies in a patient in whom a scaphoid fracture is suspected involves
four standard radiographic views: a standard PA view of the wrist, a PA view of the wrist
in ulnar deviation (scaphoid view), a lateral view, and a 45° pronated wrist oblique view
of the scaphoid. Among all diagnosed scaphoid fractures, initial radiographs are
interpreted as normal in as many as 22% of patients.17
No consensus exists on the management of the suspected scaphoid fractures.
Traditionally, patients were immobilized in a short arm cast and evaluated via repeat
imaging studies and a clinical examination after 1 or 2 weeks.18-20 Advanced imaging
studies may be considered to avoid a period of unnecessary immobilization and
restrictions.

The radiographic criteria for diagnosis of displacement are more than 1 mm of
translation and/or gapping or a radiolunate angle greater than 15°.
Advanced Imaging Studies

Advanced Imaging Studies
The use of MRI and CT to assess suspected scaphoid fractures (scaphoid tenderness
after injury with normal radiographs) is a subject of debate. Some studies advocate for
MRI in patients in whom a scaphoid fracture is suspected because a negative MRI may
provide reassurance to the patient and clinician as they navigate return to physical
activity for work and/or sport. Although this approach may reduce the risk of a missed
scaphoid fracture and avoid unnecessary immobilization, opponents of this strategy cite
high imaging costs, limited availability of MRI, high false-positive results, and
overtreatment as concerns.18,20-24
MRI is associated with a 98% sensitivity in the diagnosis of true fractures in patients in
whom a scaphoid fracture is suspected;25 however, this is more complex than such a
statement implies. A consensus reference standard is necessary to calculate a diagnostic
performance characteristic, such as specificity, sensitivity, negative predictive value, and
positive predictive value. No consensus reference standard exists for delineating bone
bruise from other signal abnormalities and fracture on MRI. False-positive results have
been documented via MRI in uninjured individuals.26 (Figure 6) In addition, because the
prevalence of true fractures in patients in whom a scaphoid fracture is suspected is low
(approximately 5% in the United States and 15% in the Netherlands), this may lead to a
low Bayes adjusted positive predictive values, even for a very sensitive and specific test.

Because of the low prevalence of true fractures in patients in whom a scaphoid fracture
is suspected, the Bayes adjusted negative predictive value is near 99% for MRI.
Therefore, the traditional goal of an all-or-nothing diagnosis of a scaphoid fracture may
be unreachable. A more prudent method may be for surgeons and patients to consider
an acceptable probability of a missed fracture. The negative predictive value of CT and
MRI are higher than 98%. The less than 2% probability of a missed fracture appears to be
acceptable.
A successful strategy in Fife, Scotland, involves the use of a virtual pathway in which
patients who sustain a low-energy fall are treated via a removable splint, instructed to
wean from splint use as pain permits, and offered the option of hand surgical
management at follow-up. This model was successful in the patient population studied,
resulting in high levels of patient satisfaction, excellent patient-reported outcome
measures, and no documented cases of symptomatic nonunion at 1 year postinjury.27
This model is associated with an implicit risk of missed scaphoid fractures but has
resulted in excellent outcomes to date.

CT often is more accessible and allows for assessment of displacement and stability.28
Displacement represents malalignment. On radiographs, this includes more than 1 mm
of translation and/or gapping or a radiolunate angle greater than 15°.29 CT can further
define dorsal or volar gapping and angular displacement. Instability represents the
movability of a fracture.30 Herbert and Fisher31 described instability in scaphoid
fractures as a complete fracture through the waist and incomplete fractures as stable.
The accuracy of CT in the diagnosis of displacement and instability was investigated via
intraoperative arthroscopy as a reference standard. Arthroscopic displacement was
defined as malalignment (gapping, translation, and/or angulation of the fracture), and
instability was defined as movement of the fracture fragments. Among 22 displaced
fractures according to radiographs and CT scans, 7 were deemed unstable via
arthroscopy. All 22 radiographically displaced fractures were unstable (mobile) during
arthroscopy. The reported accuracy of CT in the diagnosis of displacement and instability
was 82% and 70%, respectively.31 Fracture comminution (particularly a separate radial
fragment)32,33 and associated ligamentous injuries are unstable patterns.34
CT provides the best visualization of bony deformity (ie, humpback deformity) and also
may be helpful in planning for bone grafting procedures for nonunion.35 Commonly
referenced CT-based measurements for loss of alignment of the scaphoid include the
lateral intra-scaphoid angle and the height-to-length ratio of the scaphoid36,37 (Figure 7).
The reliability of these measurements is moderate and somewhat better for the height-
to-length ratio compared with other measures.37-39

Several studies have questioned the reliability of interpretations of union derived from
radiographs and, more recently, CT scans.40,41 A study measured moderate agreement
among 145 observers with regard to degrees of partial union of 13 nondisplaced
scaphoid waist fractures who used CT for evaluation.42 The negative predictive value of
CT in detecting union—meaning a diagnosis of nonunion was actually a nonunion—was
only 41%.41
A combination of a patient history, physical examination, and imaging studies helps
establish the diagnosis of a scaphoid fracture. Newer technologies involving the use of
machine learning algorithms may further improve the detection of occult scaphoid
fractures and will play a role in the future diagnosis of scaphoid fractures.

Management
Distal Tubercle Fractures
The distal part of the scaphoid is relatively well vascularized.
Distal tubercle fractures can be managed similar to a wrist sprain; a wrist splint can be used
for comfort and can be gradually weaned.

Distal Tubercle Fractures
Most fractures in the distal aspect of the scaphoid involve the distal scaphoid tubercle.43
Typically, these fractures heal uneventfully with the use of a splint for comfort, which can
be gradually weaned.44 In a relatively large series with long-term follow-up, one
asymptomatic nonunion occurred among 41 fractures.43 Wrist function was normal 10
years postinjury. Slight STT joint arthritis was observed in 7 of 41 patients,43 which
should be interpreted with the understanding that STT arthritis is common in the general
population as individuals age.45
Nondisplaced Waist Fractures
CT-verified nondisplaced fractures heal with nonsurgical management.
CT assessment of these fractures was associated with more than 50% trabecular bridging in
171 (99.4%) nondisplaced fractures of 172 during some point in the course of nonsurgical
management. This was diagnosed within a mean of 7.5 weeks and within 6 weeks in 98
fractures (57%).46 The one patient with a nonunion did not undergo an initial CT scan in the
planes defined by the long axis of the scaphoid, smoked two packs of cigarettes per day, and
had notable progressive collapse over the first year—more than that for a typical nonunion,
making this patient appear to be a true outlier. Surgical management was considered at the
1-year mark but ultimately not pursued.
In another study, CT at 4 weeks was used to diagnose displacement and union of a
radiographically diagnosed scaphoid waist fracture. Among the 43 nondisplaced fractures, 25
(58%) were diagnosed as united, and immobilization was discontinued. None of these 43
fractures were immobilized for more than 8 weeks, and all the fractures united. Eleven of 14

moderately displaced (appears to indicate angulated) fractures and the 2 severely displaced
fractures did not heal.47
Some surgeons advocate for surgical fixation to decrease immobilization and allow for earlier
return to work.
Debate exists regarding return to sports activity or heavy work after screw fixation. Some
surgeons believe that such activities should be delayed until adequate healing occurs
regardless of the treatment option selected.
If these high union rates with short immobilization times for nondisplaced fractures can be
confirmed, the potential advantages of surgical management are diminished.
Surgical management is associated with adverse events. A prominent screw requiring
revision surgery is a commonly encountered complication.
The potential advantages and risk of surgical and nonsurgical management can be presented
to a patient with a nondisplaced scaphoid waist fracture to help them make a decision
consistent with their priorities and not clouded by surgeon or patient misconceptions.

Nondisplaced Waist Fractures
The role of surgical management rather than cast immobilization is a subject of debate.
Stable, aligned waist fractures that are adequately protected almost always heal. A study
of cast immobilization in 23 patients with CT-diagnosed nondisplaced waist fractures
documented union on CT scans within 6 weeks in 21 patients (90%), with eventual union
of all fractures and no advantage noted in a comparison group of 15 fractures managed
surgically.32
Screw fixation of a nondisplaced scaphoid waist fracture can be accomplished via a volar
or dorsal percutaneous approach. Recent meta-analyses suggest a faster return to work
and faster time to union.48,49 The stated benefits of surgical fixation are worth
considering. Return to work is directed by the surgeon and may be biased. Time to union
is a questionable outcome measure given that radiographic diagnosis is associated with
limited reliability and should be interpreted with care. Other key features of the evidence
to date that leave room for debate include the absence of distinction between displaced
and nondisplaced fractures, variable diagnosis of displacement if displacement is an

inclusion criterion, the heterogenicity of surgical management (open, percutaneous), and
evaluation of union (clinical, radiographic, or CT).
A randomized, prospective trial that compared surgical and nonsurgical management of
radiographically nondisplaced scaphoid fractures in 25 US Navy personnel (11 patients in
the surgical group, 14 patients in the immobilization group) found no difference in wrist
range of motion, grip strength, or union rate between the two groups.15 Surgical
management was associated with a faster return to duty, but this was largely because
the US Navy states that individuals cannot return to duty in a cast.
A 2008 randomized controlled trial of 60 patients with a scaphoid waist fracture (7
diagnosed as displaced on radiographs) found that surgical management was associated
with more rapid return to work (3.8 weeks with surgical management versus 11 weeks
with cast immobilization) and sports activity (6.4 weeks with surgical management versus
15 weeks with cast immobilization).50
A large, multicenter randomized controlled trial of patients (n = 439) with a scaphoid
waist fracture diagnosed with minimal displacement (<2 mm) confirmed via CT
compared two treatment strategies: cast immobilization with the use of a below-elbow
cast for 6 to 10 weeks with or without the thumb and immediate surgical
management.51 Seventeen of the 195 patients treated nonsurgically assessed at 6 to 12
weeks had incomplete healing observed on CT scans and underwent surgical fixation at
that time. No substantial difference in union and employment days lost was noted
between the two groups (median of 5 employment days lost in the surgical cohort
compared with 4 employment days lost in the cast immobilization cohort). Fewer
nonunions occurred in the surgical cohort that in the cast immobilization cohort (four
versus nine, respectively; 3% overall); however, this difference was not statistically
significant. This is a relatively high nonunion rate and may be related to the inclusion of
fractures with more than 1 mm of displacement. In addition, a high incidence (65%) of
screw penetration was reported in the surgical cohort, resulting in a 4% revision surgery
rate.
The authors of this lesson diagnose displacement on CT scans if management is
initiated. Displaced fractures are managed surgically, and nondisplaced fractures are

managed with the use of a thumb spica cast. A CT scan is obtained 6 weeks postinjury.
Approximately 60% of nondisplaced scaphoid waist fractures are diagnosed with
incipient union at that time (defined as bone crossing more than 50% of the fracture
line), and immobilization is discontinued.32,46,47 If bone is crossing less than 50% of the
fracture line, immobilization is continued, and repeat CT scans are obtained in 4 to 6
weeks. The role of this additional immobilization is a subject of debate. This continued
immobilization and repeat imaging studies is based on the rationale that bone crossing
at least 50% of the fracture line allows for safe normal daily function. This is a speculative
concept that is not used for other bones in the body, in which any amount of bone
crossing the fracture site is considered union, and lacks experimental support.
Immobilization is discontinued by 12 weeks irrespective of CT scan findings. If
immobilization is discontinued, the patient is changed to a splint for comfort that is
gradually weaned, and exercises to stretch the wrist are initiated. Stable nondisplaced
waist fractures rarely progress to nonunion.46 Regardless, if no advancement of union is
observed on consecutive CT scans obtained 6 weeks apart, patients are offered
percutaneous screw fixation; however, no experimental evidence shows that this
improves union rates or outcomes.
For CT-documented nondisplaced scaphoid waist fractures, the documented benefit of
earlier return to activity may be an artifact of surgeon attitude rather than improved
physiology. In addition, the reported earlier union rate must be considered unreliable
and potentially inaccurate given knowledge of the interpretation of imaging studies.
Nondisplaced fractures that are adequately protected result in healing. Shorter and less
rigid immobilization may be adequate for these fractures. Patients treated nonsurgically
have an essentially normal wrist after recovery. Surgical management is associated with
adverse events, many of which are related to screw prominence; therefore, the relative
appeal of surgical management may be limited. Patients can select treatment with
awareness of this current best evidence. Clinicians should correct common
misconceptions and work to limit the influence of their own beliefs and biases.

Displaced Waist Fractures
A displaced or unstable scaphoid waist fracture likely will have trouble healing and
should be managed via reduction and surgical fixation to restore scaphoid alignment
and carpal kinematics and facilitate union. Depending on surgeon preference, this can

The most common fixation technique is placement of a single screw within the

pitch, which is intended to create some compression at the fracture site as the screw is
inserted. Other less commonly used fixation constructs include a volar plate, staples,

For a volar percutaneous approach, the wrist is extended via ulnar deviation. This
maneuver moves the trapezium, improving access to the distal pole of the scaphoid.
Under fluoroscopy with the wrist hyperextended, a guidewire for the cannulated screw

the proximal pole, assessed on imaging, and the screw length is measured. For most
screws, subtraction of 4 mm from the measured length is recommended to avoid screw

screw prominence is an avoidable complication, and short screws cause few problems in

An unstable nonunion of the scaphoid tends to result in malalignment. The altered
carpal kinematics are associated with wrist arthritis that progresses slowly over years to

Osteonecrosis

Osteonecrosis
The tenuous blood supply of the scaphoid makes it prone to osteonecrosis postinjury,
especially in the proximal pole because of the retrograde blood supply. If osteonecrosis
is present at the time of surgical management of nonunion, a vascularized bone graft
may be considered but is a subject of debate. This is highlighted by Rancy et al,56 who
showed that current evidence in the prediction of osteonecrosis via radiographs, CT
scans, or MRIs is poor. Although various modalities exist to assess vascularity, the
reference standard of punctate bleeding makes the accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity
indeterminate. In addition, current evidence does not support improved union rates for
vascularized bone graft compared with traditional non-vascularized bone grafting
techniques for the management of scaphoid nonunion with concomitant diagnosis of
osteonecrosis of the proximal pole. Future studies comparing reconstruction techniques
should include more reliable and accurate measures of vascularity (such as histologic
quantification of necrosis), structural defects, and proximal fragment size to better
define patients who may benefit from a vascularized procedure. In patients in whom
salvage options are being considered, proximal row carpectomy, partial carpal
arthrodesis with scaphoid excision, and total wrist arthrodesis are options.

Surgical Complications
Errors in screw length and screw positioning are the most common complications of the
surgical management of scaphoid fractures.
Debate exists regarding placement of the screw along the longitudinal axis or
perpendicular to the fracture; however, given the orientation of most fractures, this is
the same. To ensure the screw is in the bone, surgeons should aim for the long axis.
Screw length complications can be limited by selecting a screw length well shorter than
the measured length, particularly for nondisplaced fractures. Bedi and Jebson57
recommended subtracting 4 mm from the measured screw length to avoid screw
prominence. In the experience of the authors of this lesson, subtracting 6 to 8 mm does
not detract from the ability to attain fixation across the fracture site and affords a
greater margin of safety from prominent hardware.
Perilunate Injuries
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
The lunate is bound to the carpus by stout radiolunate ligaments.
A perilunate dislocation (PLD) occurs if the carpus dislocates around the lunate.
The capitate usually dislocates dorsally with respect to the lunate, causing a dorsal PLD, or
dislocates palmarly, causing a volar PLD (rare).
The sequence of injury propagates in a radial-to-ulnar direction about the lunate.
A reverse perilunate is a distinct pattern involving a dorsal dislocation of the triquetrum and
capitate and relative sparing of the scapholunate relationship (ulnar to radial sequence).
A lunate dislocation occurs if the lunate dislocates from the radial fossa palmarly, resulting in a
palmar lunate dislocation (common), or dislocates dorsally, resulting in dorsal lunate
dislocation (rare).
Fractures may pass through any bone within the greater arc of the wrist, including the distal
radius, scaphoid, trapezium, capitate, hamate, and triquetrum.
Lesser arc injuries pass only through ligamentous structures, with no corresponding fractures.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
PLDs and PLFDs are thought to result from forceful extension, ulnar deviation, and
intercarpal supination. The sequence of injury propagates in an ulnar direction about the
lunate, first rupturing the SLIL or fracturing the scaphoid, after which the capitate
fractures or dislocates from its articulation with the lunate through the space of Poirier
(between the volar radiocapitate and volar radiotriquetral ligaments) and then ruptures
the lunotriquetral ligament or fractures the triquetrum. Finally, the dorsal radiocarpal
ligament fails, allowing the lunate to rotate about its proximal volar attachments and
dislocate into the carpal tunnel (Resource 4).
Dorsal PLDs involve dorsal dislocation of the capitate with respect to the lunate as the
lunate remains in its normal position in the lunate fossa. In a lunate dislocation (ie, the
final stage of perilunate injury), the capitate has reduced from its dorsally dislocated
position to become colinear with the radius, whereas the lunate has dislocated into the
carpal tunnel. Herzberg et al58 classified PLDs as stage I injuries and lunate dislocations
as stage II injuries. Lunate dislocations are subclassified as stage IIA if the lunate has
subluxated out of its fossa but has rotated less than 90° or stage IIB injuries, which
exhibit lunate rotation greater than 90°. Volar perilunate and dorsal lunate dislocations
have been reported but are not as common. A reverse or ulnar-sided perilunate pattern
of destabilization occurs if an extended wrist hits the ground on the hypothenar mold,
which may twist the distal row into further extension; radial deviation and carpal
pronation may follow.59 A progressive pattern of ligament disruption may appear,
starting at the lunotriquetral joint (stage I), followed by complete dorsal dislocation of
the capitate (stage II) and disruption of the scapholunate joint (stage III; Figure 16 and
Figure 17).

Associated Injuries
The high-energy force propagating through the carpus during a perilunate injury may
travel through soft tissues, disrupting ligaments (ie, scapholunate, lunotriquetral,
radiocarpal); through bones, causing fractures (ie, radial styloid, scaphoid, capitate,

fracture are termed greater arc injuries, whereas those with purely ligamentous
disruption are called lesser arc injuries. In naming greater arc injuries, the prefix trans- is
used before the name of the fractured bone. For example, perilunate injuries that occur
in combination with a scaphoid fracture would be termed a trans-scaphoid PLFD. The
term translunate arc has been used to describe the rare, usually high-energy injury in
which a PLD occurs in a patient with a lunate fracture.
A variation of a perilunate injury occurs in patients with scaphocapitate syndrome, which
involves a specific greater arc injury pattern in which the force passes from the scaphoid
to the capitate neck, resulting in scaphoid and capitate fractures. The proximal pole of
the capitate undergoes considerable displacement and rotation of 90° to 180° in the
sagittal plane.60-62 ORIF via a dorsal approach is recommended (Figure 18).

Evidence of a perilunate injury on radiographs may be subtle; however, standard PA and
lateral radiographs typically are sufficient to diagnose most injuries.
On PA radiographs, the arcs of Gilula should be carefully scrutinized for any
discontinuity. The arcs of Gilula refer to curves produced by the anatomic alignment of
the bones within the carpal rows. The first arc represents the proximal convexity of the
triquetrum, lunate, and scaphoid. The second arc represents the concave distal surfaces

disruption or gapping of these arcs should increase suspicion for ligamentous or bony
injury. In addition, PA radiographs may demonstrate asymmetric widening of the
intercarpal spaces, loss of carpal height, flexion of the scaphoid (scaphoid ring sign),
and/or a triangle-shaped lunate (piece of pie sign).63,64

lunate, and capitate. In PLDs, the lunate and radius remain collinear; however, the

Acute presentation
Closed reduction may be performed initially to alleviate pain and minimize neurologic
symptoms; however, surgical management is the definitive treatment option. Multiple
reduction attempts should be avoided.
Surgeon should maintain a high index of suspicion for acute carpal tunnel syndrome and
forearm compartment syndrome, which may develop over hours to days.
If the injury has been reduced (via closed reduction) and no features of acute carpal tunnel
syndrome or ulnar translocation are present, then a dorsal approach may be adequate, and
surgical management can be planned. If surgical management is delayed, patients are
monitored for median nerve symptoms.

Management
Although surgical management is the mainstay of management for perilunate injuries,
initial prompt closed reduction is advised to decrease pressure on critical neurovascular
structures and cartilage, especially in patients with acute carpal tunnel symptoms. This
should be performed in a gentle manner, and multiple closed reduction attempts should
be avoided. Therefore, a focus on adequate sedation and relaxation should be
paramount before attempting reduction.
Closed reduction is performed with the elbow flexed to 90° and the hand placed in finger
traps. Ten to 15 lbs of longitudinal traction are applied for at least 10 minutes. Dorsal
PLDs are reduced by initially exaggerating the deformity via wrist extension and applying
traction. The wrist is then flexed through the midcarpal joint as the lunate is stabilized
palmarly. If reduction is successful, a palpable clunk usually occurs. If the lunate is
dislocated, such as in stage IIA dislocations, the wrist typically should be placed in flexion
initially to release tension on the volar ligaments. This is followed by dorsally directed
pressure on the lunate, reducing it into the lunate fossa. After reduction of the lunate, a
reduction maneuver similar to that described previously is performed while maintaining
a volar buttress on the lunate, which should reduce the capitate back onto the lunate.
After reduction, a sugar tong splint should be applied.

A dorsal approach may be used in isolation or in combination with a volar approach.
Surgical sequence generally includes:
Osseous fixation
K-wires, headless compression screws
Carpal reduction with stabilization
K-wires, screws
A midcarpal pin can be placed for adjunct stability.

Consider a carpal tunnel release with or without volar ligament repair via a separate volar

Approach
The approach used in the surgical management of these injuries varies. Isolated dorsal,
isolated volar, and combined approaches have been described with comparable
outcomes. The dorsal approach affords excellent exposure of the proximal carpal row
and the midcarpal joints. Proponents of the combined dorsal and volar approach feel
that the added volar approach improves exposure, the ease of reduction, access to distal

A dorsal approach used for the management of PLDs and PLFDs typically is performed
via a longitudinal incision centered immediately ulnar to the Lister tubercle in line with
the third metacarpal. With this approach, the skin incision is made and flaps are created,
protecting the superficial branch of the radial and ulnar nerves. The third extensor

septations between the three to four and the four to five extensor compartments. A
ligament-sparing capsulotomy is performed, exposing the scaphoid, midcarpal joint, and
radiocarpal joints (Figure 20).

symptoms of median nerve dysfunction. The authors of this lesson recommend that
patients with severe displacement of fracture fragments or fragments within the carpal

volar approach for open reduction, ligamentous stabilization, and carpal tunnel
decompression. If the carpal tunnel is not released intraoperatively, postoperative
neurologic status must be closely monitored.

Surgical Technique
Surgical management of PLDs and PLFDs includes open reduction, ligament repair, and
supplemental fixation. The surgical maxim for greater arc injuries is fixation of bony
involvement before soft-tissue repair. Scaphoid fractures typically are fixed via
cannulated headless compression screw systems. Comminuted fractures can be
managed via K-wire fixation and autologous bone grafting from the distal radius. If
concomitant scaphoid fracture and SLIL injury are present, both injuries should be

Fracture of the radial styloid should be managed via rigid fixation with the use of
cannulated screws, headless screws, K-wires, or radial column plates. Excision of the
radial styloid is not recommended. Any extruded carpal bone should be reduced to its
anatomic position and stabilized, with ligamentous repair performed to achieve a stable
wrist after healing.
Many surgeons feel that repair of the SLIL is the most critical aspect of the management
of lesser arc injuries. The ligament typically avulses from the scaphoid, and repair is
commonly performed with the use of suture anchors, with a horizontal mattress suture
through the SLIL. Unicortical K-wires can be used as joysticks to aid in reduction.
Traditionally, K-wires were used to protect the SLIL repair. Initial passage of these K-
wires antegrade while the carpus is dislocated may be helpful, with finalization of the
construct via retrograde insertion after anatomic reduction of the carpus is achieved;
however, concerns for pin tract infection, soft-tissue irritation, delayed motion, inability
to provide compression, and biomechanical weakness have led some surgeons to
advocate for more rigid fixation of the scapholunate interval.
Temporary intercarpal screw fixation and intraosseous cerclage wiring have been
described as methods for protection of the soft-tissue repair. Theoretic advantages
include subdermal location, decreased infection risk, increased biomechanical stability,
and the ability to impart compression. Potential disadvantages include the need for a
secondary surgical procedure and difficult implant placement. Results with these
methods are comparable to those of K-wire fixation (Figure 21).

These injuries are considered wrist sprains and are managed symptomatically, typically with
optional immobilization for comfort for approximately 4 weeks.

Capitate Fractures
Similar to the scaphoid bone, the capitate is covered mainly by cartilage.
Capitate head fractures and displaced neck fractures benefit from surgical management.
Nondisplaced fractures can be managed nonsurgically via short arm cast immobilization for 4
to 8 weeks.

Capitate Fractures
The capitate, similar to the scaphoid, is covered mostly in articular cartilage and is
relatively protected within the carpus. The vascularity of the capitate recently has been
shown to be robust because approximately 70% of the capitate has additional proximal
vessels that limit the risk of osteonecrosis after fracture.67
The capitate is commonly fractured after a fall onto an extended wrist in ulnar deviation;
however, fracture can occur with an axial load through the base of the third metacarpal.
A review of capitate fractures over a 13-year period identified 43 adult patients. Of these
patients, 22 patients had an avulsion fracture, 5 patients had a bone contusion, 10
patients had a perilunate injury, and 6 patients had an isolated fracture.61
Nondisplaced fractures are managed via short arm cast immobilization for 4 to 8
weeks.68 Displaced fractures are managed with the use of headless screws.69

It can be diagnosed by carefully scrutinizing radiographs; however, CT may aid in diagnosis.

Carpometacarpal Fracture-Dislocations
CMC fracture-dislocation commonly occurs at the ring and little fingers. The mechanism
of injury typically involves high-energy trauma; direct punching (54%), motor vehicle
collisions (23%), and falls (14%) are the most common causes.70
Pain and swelling to the dorsum of the hand typically accompany these injuries.
Occasionally, a bump on the dorsum of the hand may be visible from the dorsal
subluxation of the metacarpal base. Oblique radiographs with pronation and supination
may aid in visualizing alignment of the radial and ulnar CMC joints, respectively.71 CT
may aid in diagnosis and assessment.
These injuries usually are accompanied by shearing or intra-articular compression
fractures of the hamate or capitate.
Primary treatment goals are to restore the articular anatomy of the fourth and fifth CMC
joints to preserve mobility and limit posttraumatic arthritis.
Initial closed management followed by nonsurgical immobilization in a short dorsal arm
splint for 1 month is reserved for small marginal fractures.
Surgical management is recommended for larger, displaced fractures. Closed reduction
with percutaneous pinning is an option if an anatomic reduction is attained but difficult
to maintain; however, open reduction often is necessary for these injury patterns to
attain a satisfactory reduction of articular impaction. After reduction is attained, fracture
fixation is performed with the use of compression screws or low-profile plates, and
articular stabilization is achieved with the use of K-wires.69

Hamate Fractures
Hook of hamate fractures are common in racket-sport athletes, baseball players, and golfers.
The proximity of the ulnar nerve should warrant careful neurovascular examination in patients
in whom these injuries are suspected.
Nondisplaced hook of hamate fractures can be managed nonsurgically.
Displaced fractures and symptomatic nonunions can be managed via hook excision.

Hamate Fractures
The hamate is the most ulnar carpal bone of the distal carpal row and contains a volar
projection known as the hook of hamate. The hook of hamate is immediately radial to
the ulnar neurovascular, forming one of the sites of attachment for the transverse carpal
ligament.68
Direct compression of the ulnar side of the palm is the most frequent mechanism of
injury for hook fractures. This injury is commonly observed in individuals who participate
in racket sports, baseball players, and golfers. After injury, pain often is elicited via
palpation over the hamate and with gripping or resisted flexion of the little and ring
fingers70 (Figure 24).
